==Problem==
Forty slips of paper numbered <math>1</math> to <math>40</math> are placed in a hat. Alice and Bob each draw one number from the hat without replacement, keeping their numbers hidden from each other. Alice says, "I can't tell who has the larger number." Then Bob says, "I know who has the larger number." Alice says, "You do? Is your number prime?" Bob replies, "Yes." Alice says, "In that case, if I multiply your number by <math>100</math> and add my number, the result is a perfect square. " What is the sum of the two numbers drawn from the hat?

<math>\textbf{(A) }27\qquad\textbf{(B) }37\qquad\textbf{(C) }47\qquad\textbf{(D) }57\qquad\textbf{(E) }67</math>
== Solution 1 ==
Let Alice have the number A, Bob B.
When Alice says that she can't tell who has the larger number, it means that <imath>A</imath> cannot equal <imath>1</imath>. Therefore, it makes sense that Bob has <imath>2</imath> because he now knows that Alice has the larger number. <imath>2</imath> is also prime. The last statement means that <imath>200+A</imath> is a perfect square. The three squares in the range <imath>200-300</imath> are <imath>225</imath>, <imath>256</imath>, and <imath>289</imath>. So, <imath>A</imath> could equal <imath>25</imath>, <imath>56</imath>, or <imath>89</imath>, so <imath>A+B</imath> is <imath>27</imath>, <imath>58</imath>, or <imath>91</imath>, of only <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(A) }27}</imath> is below <imath>40</imath>, therefore it is the correct answer since the maximum number one can have is 40.

--stjwyl

== Solution 2==
Denote by <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> the numbers drawn by Alice and Bob, respectively.

Alice's sentence “I can't tell who has the larger number.” implies <math>A \in \left\{ 2 , \cdots , 39 \right\}</math>.

Bob's sentence “I know who has the larger number.” implies <math>B \in \left\{ 1 , 2 , 39, 40 \right\}</math>.

Their subsequent conversation that <math>B</math> is prime implies <math>B = 2</math>.

Then, Alice's next sentence  “In that case, if I multiply your number by 100 and add my number, the result is a perfect square.” implies <math>200 + A</math> is a perfect square.
Hence, <math>A = 25</math>.

Therefore, the answer is <math>\boxed{\textbf{(A) }27}</math>.

~Steven Chen (www.professorchenedu.com)

== Solution 3 - Guessing those Squares == 

We see that <imath>225</imath> is one such square that works. Bob gets <imath>2</imath> and Alice gets <imath>25</imath> which is valid. Thus, <imath>2 + 25 = 27.</imath> So <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(A) }27}</imath> is our answer.

-D1r

==Solution 4 (Ambiguity, Sanity Checks)==

The MAA knows this problem is ambiguous, as the interpretation of what might be viewed as the "middle" of the set could be different for all. Then, they would have specifically designed the answer choices such that one choice is guaranteed to be correct while all others are unobtainable. 

So, for a sanity check and our general satisfaction, we will use the set <imath>\mathcal{A} \in \{5,6,7,\dots,34,35 \}</imath> as all the possible values of <imath>\mathcal{A}</imath> and <imath>\mathcal{B} \in \{1,2,3,4,36,37,38,39,40 \}</imath>. Alice notes that Bob's number is prime. Therefore, <imath>\mathcal{B} \in \{2,3,4,37\}</imath>. Now, say Alice's number is <imath>A</imath>. Then, each of <imath>200+A</imath>, <imath>300+A</imath>, and <imath>3700+A</imath> is prime. Note that in each case, <imath>A = 25, 24, 21</imath> respectively. Then, <imath>A+B = 27, 27, 58</imath> respectively. Only <imath>\boxed{27}</imath> is in the answer choices, so that would be our answer.

~Pinotation

==Sidenote==
Note that Bob's statement (that he knows who won/lost) comes after Alice tells him that she doesn't know who won. Since Alice doesn't know who won, Bob knows that she didn't get draw a <math>1</math> (or a <math>40</math>), which tells him that his <math>2</math> must be lower than Alice's number. 

~jd9
